versions.question: An order event must trigger an email, a Lambda function and three queues, and the producer should make a single call. What do you use?
options: A Kinesis stream with five readers
An SQS queue read by each target
An SNS topic with five subscriptions
Separate API calls to each target
versions.explanation: SNS is pub/sub: every subscription gets every message unless a filter policy says otherwise.
option_explanations: Consumers pull; a stream can't email anyone.
Each message is taken by one consumer only.
Correct. One publish, a copy per subscription.
The producer would integrate with every target.

versions.question: One message from a producer has to land at many different receivers at once. Which model fits?
versions.explanation: Pub/sub decouples the producer from how many receivers exist and what they are.
option_explanations: Couples receivers to a database and adds delay.

versions.question: Which endpoint types can an SNS topic deliver to? (Choose 4)
versions.explanation: Protocols: SQS, Lambda, Firehose, HTTP/S, email, SMS and mobile push.

versions.question: A team wants SNS to notify several targets. Which can a subscription use? (Choose 3)
versions.explanation: S3 is a common SNS publisher, but not a subscriber.
option_explanations: To reach S3, go through Firehose.
SNS can reach Firehose, not Data Streams.

versions.question: Pick the accurate statements about SNS standard topics. (Choose 2)
options: Subscribers can replay last week's messages
Messages are pushed and not kept afterwards
One topic can hold millions of subscriptions
Each topic is limited to 100 subscribers
versions.explanation: Put SQS behind SNS when messages must survive a consumer outage.
option_explanations: The real limit is in the millions.

versions.question: A subscriber to an SNS standard topic with no DLQ was down for an hour. What happens to messages it missed once retries run out?
versions.explanation: SNS retries per its delivery policy; after that, only a DLQ or an SQS subscriber keeps the message.
option_explanations: SNS has no message retention on standard topics.
Correct. A subscription DLQ (an SQS queue) would have kept them.

versions.question: Which SNS API call delivers one message to every subscription of a topic?
versions.explanation: Publish targets a topic ARN (or a mobile platform endpoint).
option_explanations: SQS: writes up to 10 messages to one queue.
Kinesis: writes records to a stream.

versions.question: A developer called SQS SendMessage with a topic ARN and got an error. What should the code call instead?
versions.explanation: SQS and SNS have separate APIs: SendMessage for queues, Publish for topics.
option_explanations: Correct. The SNS call for topics.

versions.question: Which controls protect data and access on an SNS topic? (Choose 3)
options: Server-side encryption with a KMS key
Encryption done for you on the client
versions.explanation: Same model as SQS: IAM policies plus a resource policy on the topic.
option_explanations: NACLs apply to subnets, not topics.
Client-side encryption is your own code.

versions.question: S3 in the same account must publish event notifications to an SNS topic. What grants it permission?
options: An SCP attached to the account
versions.explanation: Service principals like S3 need the topic's resource policy to allow them.
option_explanations: Bucket ACLs control access to the bucket.
SCPs only limit permissions; they don't grant them.

versions.question: Orders must reach a billing queue and a warehouse queue without loss, and a third queue joins next month. How do you wire it?
options: Have the app call SendMessage twice
Subscribe each queue to one SNS topic
Point both services at one queue
Stream orders into S3 via Firehose
versions.explanation: SNS + SQS fan-out: SQS adds persistence, SNS adds the copies.
option_explanations: A crash between calls leaves one queue without the order.
Correct. Adding a queue is just a new subscription.
Each message is consumed by one service only.
Lands in storage, not in the service queues.

versions.question: In an SNS-to-SQS fan-out, nothing arrives in the queues. What's the most likely missing piece?
options: A queue policy allowing the topic
versions.explanation: Each SQS queue's access policy must allow the SNS topic ARN to write.
option_explanations: Affects re-delivery after receive, not arrival.
Affects how consumers poll, not delivery.
Correct. The queue must let the topic call SendMessage.
Standard topics deliver to standard queues.

versions.question: Each new object in a bucket should be handled by three queues, but the bucket's notification rules can't overlap. What's the approach?
options: Point the notification at an SNS topic
Have each queue forward to the next
Have the first consumer forward it
versions.explanation: S3 → SNS → SQS is the classic fix for the one-rule-per-event-and-prefix limit.
option_explanations: Correct. All three queues subscribe to the topic.
Overlapping rules aren't a quota you can raise.
SQS queues can't forward to each other.
Couples consumers and fails if that one is down.

versions.question: An S3 PUT event must reach queues A, B and C. Which destination do you set on the bucket?
options: Queue A, which forwards to B and C
An SNS topic for all three
A Kinesis stream read by all three
Three rules with the same prefix
versions.explanation: Each queue needs a policy allowing the SNS topic to send to it.

versions.question: A payment event goes to several services that each need strict per-account order and no duplicates. Which setup?
versions.explanation: Use the account ID as the message group ID to keep per-account order.
option_explanations: SNS standard topics can't deliver to FIFO queues.
Correct. Order per message group, deduplication.
Each message would reach only one service.

versions.question: What does an SNS FIFO topic use to keep related messages in order?
versions.explanation: SNS FIFO mirrors SQS FIFO: message group IDs for order, a 5-minute dedup window.
option_explanations: Correct. Plus a deduplication ID or content-based dedup.

versions.question: One topic carries orders of every status. The refunds queue should receive only status=refunded. Where do you set this?
options: A filter policy on its subscription
A message group ID for each status
A Lambda that drops the rest
A second topic the producer picks
versions.explanation: Filter policies are JSON on the subscription; they match attributes or the body.
option_explanations: Correct. SNS drops non-matching messages for that subscription.
Groups order messages; doesn't route them.
Extra code and the messages still arrive.
Pushes routing logic into the producer.

versions.question: An SNS subscription has no filter policy. Which messages does it get?
options: None until a policy is added
versions.explanation: No filter policy means the subscription receives everything published.
option_explanations: Delivery doesn't wait for a policy.

versions.question: Which subscription filter policy lets through only messages whose `state` attribute is `placed`?
versions.explanation: Each key is an attribute name; its value is an array of allowed values.
option_explanations: Key and value are swapped, and values must be arrays.
Attribute names go at the top level, with no wrapper key.
Values must be arrays; there's no equals operator.

versions.question: By default, what does SNS match a subscription's filter policy against?
versions.explanation: Set the scope to MessageBody for payload-based filtering.
option_explanations: Possible, but only if you set FilterPolicyScope to MessageBody.

versions.question: Every message on an SNS topic must also be stored in an S3 bucket, with no code to run. What do you add?
versions.explanation: SNS → Firehose → S3 is the managed archive path.
option_explanations: Works, but it's code you must run.
S3 isn't an SNS protocol; go through Firehose.
Holds messages; nothing writes them to S3.

versions.question: Which SNS subscription type can pass messages on to S3, Redshift or OpenSearch?
versions.explanation: Firehose can deliver to any of its supported destinations.

versions.question: Sensor readings must be processed as they arrive, and an analytics app added later must re-read last week's data. Which service?
versions.explanation: Default retention is 24 hours; you can raise it to 365 days.
option_explanations: Processes streams; it doesn't store them for replay.
Correct. Records stay until retention expires.

versions.question: What's the longest retention you can set on a Kinesis data stream?
versions.explanation: Records can't be deleted individually; they expire.

versions.question: Which of these can read records from a Kinesis data stream? (Choose 3)
versions.explanation: Custom apps use the KCL to read.
option_explanations: SES sends email; it doesn't read streams.

versions.question: Which tools write records into a Kinesis data stream? (Choose 2)
versions.explanation: KPL batches and retries for high throughput; KCL is the consumer side.
option_explanations: Correct. Tails log files on servers.

versions.question: Events for each user must be processed in the order they happened. What should producers set on each record?
options: A random UUID as the partition key
The timestamp as the partition key
The user ID as the partition key
versions.explanation: Order holds within a shard; the partition key picks the shard.
option_explanations: Spreads one user's events across shards.
Each event gets a different key.
Doesn't keep a user's events together.

versions.question: Kinesis Data Streams guarantees order at what level?
versions.explanation: Same partition key → same shard → ordered.
option_explanations: A consumer may read many shards.

versions.question: Producers will write 6 MB/s into a provisioned stream. What's the fewest shards that can take it?
versions.explanation: Writes: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s per shard. Reads: 2 MB/s per shard.

versions.question: A stream has 4 provisioned shards. Roughly how much can it ingest per second?
versions.explanation: Each shard: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s in, 2 MB/s out.
option_explanations: That's the read limit in MB.

versions.question: Load on a new stream could be 1 MB/s or 50 MB/s and nobody can predict it. Which setting spares the team from resizing?
versions.explanation: On-demand scales to double the previous 30-day write peak.
option_explanations: Still manual, and you pay for idle shards.

versions.question: A new on-demand stream starts with what write capacity?
versions.explanation: It then grows with your 30-day peak; pay per stream-hour plus data.
option_explanations: Too high for a new stream.
That's a shard's read limit in MB.

versions.question: Three apps read one stream and keep getting read-throttled. How can each app get dedicated read bandwidth?
versions.explanation: Enhanced fan-out uses SubscribeToShard (HTTP/2 push).
option_explanations: Shared readers still split the same read limit.
Correct. 2 MB/s per shard per consumer, pushed.
Changes write spread, not read limits.

versions.question: With standard shared consumers, how much read throughput does one shard give?
versions.explanation: Shared mode also caps GetRecords at 5 calls/s per shard.

versions.question: With CLI v2, `aws kinesis put-record --data "user signup"` fails on plain text. Which flag fixes it?
versions.explanation: CLI v2 expects blob input to be Base64 unless you set this flag.
option_explanations: Correct. Tells the CLI to Base64-encode the raw text.

versions.question: Which shard iterator type starts reading from the oldest record still in the shard?
versions.explanation: Use NextShardIterator from each GetRecords response to keep reading.
option_explanations: Starts at a time you give.

versions.question: A consumer logs a record's data field and sees `dXNlciBzaWdudXA=`. What's going on?
versions.explanation: Lambda and the raw API both hand you Base64; SDKs often decode it for you.
option_explanations: KMS decrypts transparently for allowed callers.
Correct. Decode it to get the text.
The text was fine; it's an encoding.

versions.question: Data read through the raw Kinesis API arrives in which encoding?
versions.explanation: Decode the data field before parsing it.

versions.question: App logs must land in S3 and OpenSearch within a minute or so, and the team won't run any consumer code. What do they use?
versions.explanation: Firehose = managed, serverless, near real-time delivery.
option_explanations: You'd write and run the function.
You'd write and run the worker.

versions.question: Which service loads streaming data into Redshift for you, scaling on its own, with no servers or shards to manage?
versions.explanation: Near real-time because of buffering.
option_explanations: Correct. It stages in S3 and runs COPY.

versions.question: Which can a Firehose stream deliver to? (Choose 3)
versions.explanation: Also S3, HTTP endpoints, partners like Datadog, Snowflake and Iceberg tables.
option_explanations: Firehose can read from it, not write to it.

versions.question: A team picks Firehose for log delivery. Which targets can they set? (Choose 2)
versions.explanation: Failed or all records can also be backed up to S3.

versions.question: Firehose receives CSV lines, but the destination wants JSON documents. Which feature handles it?
versions.explanation: Firehose invokes the Lambda on batches and delivers what it returns.
option_explanations: Only JSON to Parquet or ORC.
Splits data by key into prefixes.
Keeps a copy of source records.

versions.question: Firehose's built-in record format conversion turns JSON into which formats? (Choose 2)
versions.explanation: Columnar formats save space and query cost in Athena or Redshift Spectrum.

versions.question: Data sent to Firehose shows up in S3 a few minutes later. What causes the delay?
versions.explanation: The S3 default buffer is 5 MiB or 300 s, whichever comes first.
option_explanations: Firehose has no shards to manage.
Correct. It flushes on size or time.
Only if a transform is set, and it's seconds.

versions.question: Which two settings decide when Firehose flushes data to S3? (Choose 2)
versions.explanation: Whichever limit is hit first triggers delivery.

versions.question: Which is TRUE of Data Firehose but not of Kinesis Data Streams?
versions.explanation: Streams: collect and replay. Firehose: load into destinations.
option_explanations: Correct. Fully managed and auto scaling.

versions.question: Which is TRUE of Kinesis Data Streams but not of Firehose?
options: It needs no code to load S3
versions.explanation: Data Streams supports provisioned or on-demand capacity and replay.

versions.question: A Flink application on AWS needs an input stream. Which can it read? (Choose 2)
versions.explanation: Managed Service for Apache Flink was formerly Kinesis Data Analytics.
option_explanations: Firehose can be a Flink output, not an input.

versions.question: Which pipeline puts Managed Service for Apache Flink in a valid place?
versions.explanation: Flink reads Data Streams or MSK and can write to Firehose, S3 and more.

versions.question: Jobs must sit in a durable buffer until one of many workers takes each, and the worker removes it when done. Which service?
versions.explanation: SQS: pull model, scales automatically, FIFO when order matters.
option_explanations: Records stay for every reader until expiry.

versions.question: After processing an SQS message, what must a worker do so no other worker gets it?
versions.explanation: Until deleted, a message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout.
option_explanations: It reappears after the visibility timeout.
That's how KCL tracks Kinesis progress.

versions.question: A message must survive until a consumer deletes it, for up to two weeks. Which service has that persistence model?
versions.explanation: SQS: pull then delete. SNS: push. Data Streams: retain and replay.
option_explanations: Records expire; consumers can't delete them.

versions.question: Which service makes you choose provisioned shards or on-demand capacity?
versions.explanation: SQS and SNS scale with no capacity settings.

versions.question: Which SQS setting and maximum go together?
versions.explanation: Defaults: retention 4 days, visibility timeout 30 s.

versions.question: Which statement about these streaming and messaging services is accurate?
versions.explanation: Know the limits that separate SQS, SNS, Data Streams, Firehose and Flink.
option_explanations: Flink reads Data Streams or MSK.
